messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus Venn

Marcus Venn was sixty-eight years old when he was detained in a facility in Southeast Asia during what had been intended as a humanitarian technology mission. He had gone there to help a nonprofit install educational software in rural schools. The men who took him believed he was a spy. For eleven days, they kept him in a concrete room without windows, and they broke three of his fingers on his left hand to make him confess to crimes he had not committed. They did not break them all at once. The breaking was methodical, designed to wear him down between sessions of questioning. Marcus had refused to sign anything false, and so they had continued. When he was finally released through diplomatic intervention, his left hand was swollen and purple, and something inside him had fractured in a way that no X-ray could show.

That was four years ago. Marcus had returned to his apartment in Seattle, undergone physical therapy, and resumed his job at a mid-sized software firm. On the surface, he had recovered. His fingers had healed. He had not sought help immediately because he believed that what had happened was over, that it lived only in the past. But the past, he came to understand, had never actually left.

The first change was small. Marcus found himself studying the faces of people in meetings—his colleagues, the barista at the coffee shop near his office, the cashier at the grocery store. He was looking for something he could not quite name, some tell in the set of a jaw or the direction of a gaze that would warn him of danger. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost logical, that he could read threat in human expression the way other people read words on a page. At work, during a code review with a younger engineer named David, Marcus had stared so intently at David's face, searching for signs of aggression or deception, that David had asked if something was wrong. Marcus had said nothing was wrong. But it was. Something had shifted in how he perceived other people. They were no longer simply colleagues or strangers. They were potential threats that required constant decoding.

His apartment became a fortress. Marcus installed new locks on his bedroom door, then on the front door, then upgraded to a deadbolt system. Every evening, before he could allow himself to sit down, he would walk through the apartment checking the locks—first the front door, then the bedroom, then the windows, running his fingers along the frames to ensure they were secure. Some nights he would check three times. Some nights, lying in bed, he would rise and check again because the certainty would slip away and be replaced by a creeping doubt. What if he had missed something? What if a window was not actually locked? The checking would begin again.

Sleep became a negotiation with himself. Marcus would lie in the dark, acutely aware of every sound in the building—the hum of the refrigerator, a neighbor's footsteps in the hallway, the settling of the old wood frame. His body would not relax into sleep because sleep felt like surrendering his vigilance. To sleep was to be defenseless, and he was certain that defenselessness would be punished. He would lie awake for hours, his mind alert, his body tense, waiting for something he could not name.

Over time, Marcus had stopped going out except for work. Being alone in his apartment had become intolerable—the silence felt like a threat—but being around other people required the exhausting work of monitoring their faces, of staying alert. So he had narrowed his world. He went to the office because he had to, and he came home. He did not go to restaurants or movies or the park. He did not accept invitations from colleagues. One of his oldest friends, Robert, had called several times asking to meet for dinner. Marcus had declined each time, and eventually Robert had stopped calling. Marcus told himself this was better. It was safer to be apart. The people who had hurt him had been people too, and he had learned that people could not be trusted.

What troubled him most was something he could not quite control. His mind would turn to the detention, to the room, to the sound of his own voice refusing to confess to lies. He would try not to think about it—would deliberately turn his attention to work, to a television program, to anything else—but the effort of not thinking about it consumed him. And underneath all of this was a deeper, more corrosive belief: that he had compromised something essential in himself during those eleven days. He had begged them to stop, had cried, had felt terror so complete that it had unmade him. He had always thought of himself as a principled person, someone with integrity. But that person had been shattered, and what remained felt like an imposter wearing his name.

At seventy-two, Marcus had finally called a therapist. His supervisor had noticed his increasing withdrawal from team projects and had gently suggested that he might benefit from speaking to someone. Marcus had resisted for weeks. But last month, alone in his apartment on a Saturday evening, checking the locks for what felt like the hundredth time, he had realized that the life he was living was not a life at all. It was a siege. And he did not know how to end it alone.
